translationRepairs: Wang Shu, whose courtesy name was Ruolin and style name Xuzhou, came from Jintan in Jiangnan.
Wang Shu, whose courtesy name was Ruolin and sobriquet Xuzhou, came from Jintan in Jiangnan.
Chinese pairs 字若林 with 號虛舟; 號 is a sobriquet (hao), so idiomatic 'style name Xuzhou' wrongly conflates 號 with style/courtesy naming.
Later the Grand Secretary Weng Fanggang took a different view, holding that Shu's seal script preserved the ancient manner, his running script came next, and his regular script ranked below both.

Later the Academician of the Grand Secretariat Weng Fanggang took a different view, holding that Shu's seal script preserved the ancient manner, his running script came next, and his regular script ranked below both.
內閣學士 is Academician of the Grand Secretariat; Grand Secretary would be 大學士, so the idiomatic office title is wrong.
Later Grand Secretary Weng Fanggang held a different view, saying his seal script obtained ancient methods, running script was next, and regular script ranked below again.
Later Academician of the Grand Secretariat Weng Fanggang held a different view, saying his seal script obtained ancient methods, running script was next, and regular script ranked below again.
Same office error in the literal field: 內閣學士 is not Grand Secretary (大學士).

Yongxi's provincial examination came from Jiang Chenying's school; he and He Chao were both guests of Li Guangdi, and his discussions of calligraphy largely agreed and disagreed with those two houses.

Yongxi's provincial examination came from Jiang Chenying's school; he and He Chao were both guests of Li Guangdi, and his discussions of calligraphy largely agreed with, and at times diverged from, those two houses.
相出入 means his views largely agreed with yet also diverged from the two schools; 'agreed and disagreed' is contradictory English that obscures that sense.
Three years later he ranked first in the palace examination and was promoted to Hanlin reader.
Three years later he ranked first in the grand examination and was promoted to Hanlin reader.
大考 is the Hanlin ranking examination of serving academicians, not the palace examination (殿試); he had already taken the jinshi route in s0041.
His love of calligraphy came from innate nature; at twelve he could write large characters in bokou style.
His love of calligraphy came from innate nature; at twelve he could write large characters in boke style.
擘窠 (bòkē) is the large-character tablet style; 'bokou' is a corrupted romanization.
Deng Shiru, whose original given name avoided the Jiaqing Emperor's taboo and so he went by his style name, later changed his style to Wanbo, a man of Huaining in Anhui.

Deng Shiru, whose original given name conflicted with Emperor Renzong's (the Jiaqing Emperor's) personal-name taboo and who therefore went by his courtesy name, later changed his courtesy name to Wanbo; he was a man of Huaining in Anhui.

避仁宗諱 means his original given name conflicted with Emperor Renzong's taboo, so he went by his 字 (courtesy name) and later changed that courtesy name to Wanbo; 'avoided' and 'style' misstate both the taboo and 字.

He studied the Stone Drum Inscriptions, Li Si's Mount Yi and Mount Tai inscriptions, the Han Kaimu stone que, the Dunhuang prefect stele, Wu Su Jian's Guoshan stele, the Huangxiang Tianfa Shenchen stele, and Li Yangbing's City God Temple stele and Record of the Three Tombs—making a hundred copies of each.

He studied the Stone Drum Inscriptions, Li Si's Mount Yi and Mount Tai inscriptions, the Han Kaimu stone que, the Dunhuang prefect stele, Wu Su Jian's Guoshan stele, Huang Xiang's Tianfa Shenchen stele, and Tang Li Yangbing's City God Temple stele and Record of the Three Tombs—making a hundred copies of each.
皇像天發神讖碑 is Huang Xiang's Tianfa Shenchen stele, and 唐李陽冰 must keep Tang; but 吳蘇建國山碑 retains Su Jian as the Wu calligrapher of the Guoshan stele, so dropping 蘇建 is wrong.
He said of himself: 'My seal script has not reached Yang Bing, but my clerical script is not inferior to Liang He.'
He said of himself: 'My seal script has not reached Yangbing, but my clerical script is not inferior to Liang He.'
陽冰 is the undivided given name Yangbing; splitting it as Yang Bing invents a false two-syllable personal name.
Dian prided himself that his seal script directly connected with Yang Bing; once traveling to Mount Jiao he saw the Heart Sutra in seal script on a wall and sighed that it was next to Yang Bing.
Dian prided himself that his seal script descended directly from Yangbing; once traveling to Mount Jiao he saw the Heart Sutra in seal script on a wall and sighed that it was second only to Yangbing.
Both 陽冰 instances are Yangbing, not Yang Bing; 亞 means second only to, which the proposed wording restores.

Others who studied under the Bao school alongside Xizai included Mei Zhizhi of Jiangdu, Yang Liang of Ganquan, Huang Xun of Gaoliang, Mao Changling of Yuyao, Yao Peizhong of Jingde, and Yang Cheng of Songtao.

Others who studied under the Bao school alongside Xizai included Mei Zhizhi Yunsheng of Jiangdu, Yang Liang Jizi of Ganquan, Huang Xun Xiucun of Gaoliang, Mao Changling Yangsu of Yuyao, Yao Peizhong Zhongyu of Jingde, and Yang Chengwang Yizhi of Songtao.
Chinese lists each disciple with courtesy name (蘊生、季子、修存、仰蘇、仲虞、挹之) and writes 楊承汪; omitting the courtesy names and shortening to Yang Cheng drops supported naming.

Those who like Xizai received the Bao school's method included Mei Zhizhi Yunsheng of Jiangdu, Yang Liang Jizi of Ganquan, Huang Xunxiucun of Gaoliang, Mao Changling Yangsu of Yuyao, Yao Peizhong Zhongyu of Jingde, and Yang Cheng Wangyizhi of Songtao.

Those who like Xizai received the Bao school's method included Mei Zhizhi Yunsheng of Jiangdu, Yang Liang Jizi of Ganquan, Huang Xun Xiucun of Gaoliang, Mao Changling Yangsu of Yuyao, Yao Peizhong Zhongyu of Jingde, and Yang Chengwang Yizhi of Songtao.
黃洵修存 must be Huang Xun Xiucun, and 楊承汪挹之 is Yang Chengwang Yizhi; the literal fusions mis-segment both names.
He styled his dwelling Jian Hermitage.
